title: Exile
hookLine: since 1959 the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans have lived in exile; a sorrow held with care

cards: If you had one night to leave your home, and could never come back, what would you carry? Not what you'd pack. What you'd carry: the songs, the recipes, the prayers your grandmother said, the way your family does things.
In 1959, and in the years after, a great many Tibetans faced some version of that question.
Many of the practices you've met these two weeks, the chants, the mandalas, the teachers, reached the rest of the world because people carried them over the mountains.

teach.b: Here is the history, told plainly. Chinese forces entered Tibet, and in March 1959, after an uprising in Lhasa, the fourteenth Dalai Lama, still a young man, left the city at night.
He crossed the Himalayas on horseback and on foot and reached India. Many Tibetans followed him, then and in the years after.
India gave land and shelter, and the hill town of Dharamsala became the Dalai Lama's home and the seat of the Tibetan administration in exile.

People hold strong and very different views about Tibet's politics, and the Chinese government describes these events very differently. This lesson stays with the people and the practice. Here is what they carried.
Some texts came out on foot, in bundles. Others lived in the memories of monks, who recited them so they could be written down again.

teach.h: DHARAMSALA, AND FIELDS IN THE SOUTH.
teach.b: The great monasteries of Sera, Drepung and Ganden were founded anew in the fields of south India, and the debating courtyards filled with clapping and questions once more.
Settlements grew in India and Nepal, and later in Europe and North America. Teachers who would never have left Tibet began teaching in cities all over the world.
Tibetans speak of this loss with grief. The Dalai Lama has often said that those who drove them out are also to be held with compassion.
That's the sorrow held with care: not pretending it didn't happen, not letting it turn into hatred.
A tradition, carried on foot, into exile.

how: Tibetan communities in exile, centered on Dharamsala and settlements in India and Nepal, have re-founded major monasteries, schools and institutes, and many Tibetans mark March 10, the anniversary of the 1959 uprising, with prayers and gatherings.

o: a monk's retreat into the mountains
living forced away from your homeland
a long pilgrimage taken by choice

games.q: match the pieces of the exile.
p: monasteries founded anew in the south
recited so they could be written again

s: the Dalai Lama left Lhasa at night and crossed the Himalayas
on horseback and on foot, he reached India in 1959.
only a few monks followed him into exile
many Tibetans followed, then and in the years after.
the Dalai Lama has taught compassion even for those who drove them out
that's the sorrow held with care: grief without hatred.

games.q: you're a monk who has fled with nothing but your robes. your monastery's library is gone. what do you do?
o: give up on the old teachings.
recite the texts you memorized so they can be written down again.
wait until you can go back.
games.why: some texts were carried out; others were recited by monks who knew them by heart, written down again, and the monasteries rebuilt, in exile.

practice: Picture Tibetans living far from the land their families came from, an old monk in south India, a teenager in a city apartment who has never seen Tibet, and silently offer them the metta phrases you learned: may you be safe, may you be well, may you be at ease.
If you'd like, widen it to everyone, anywhere, who has had to leave home. Then rest in the breath.

wordCard.voice: Exile. Since 1959, the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans have lived outside Tibet, carrying their practice with them: a sorrow held with care.

orig.note: Pali mettā: loving-kindness, the first word of this path, offered today to those living in exile.

carryVoice: Your line: carried into exile. Grief, held with care and without hatred. That's day three hundred sixteen.
